title: I Shall Die in Paris in a Downpour…
text:
I shall die in Paris in a downpour,
+
+on a day whose memory is already mine.
+
+I shall die in Paris—and I do not flinch—
+
+perhaps a Thursday, as today is, in autumn.
+
+
+It will be Thursday, because today, Thursday, as I prose
+
+these verses, I have put my humeri on
+
+the wrong way and, never as today, have I turned,
+
+with all my road, to see myself alone.
+
+
+César Vallejo is dead; they all struck him
+
+though he did nothing to them;
+
+they hit him hard with a stick and hard
+
+
+also with a rope; witnesses are
+
+the Thursdays and the humerus bones,
+
+the solitude, the rain, the roads…
editorial_note: The prophetic future folds into a remembered death; proso is made a verb as prose, and the awkwardly worn humeri preserve Vallejo’s fusion of grammar, anatomy, and isolation.

title: Trilce: Poem LXIX — What Do You Seek from Us, O Sea
text:
What do you seek from us, O sea, with your
+teaching volumes! How inconsolable, how atrocious
+you are in the feverish suntrap.
+
+With your hoes you leap,
+with your leaves you leap,
+axing, axing in mad sesame,
+while the waves return weeping, after
+unshoeing the four winds
+and all memories, in lipped platters
+of tungsten, contractions of fangs
+and static chelonian els.
+
+Philosophy of black wings vibrating
+at the fearful trembling of the day’s shoulders.
+
+The sea, and an edition standing,
+upon its single sheet the recto
+facing the verso.
editorial_note: Volumes and hojas retain the sea’s simultaneous book and material mass; descalcar becomes unshoeing, while the typographic els remain turtle-like chelonians.

title: Trilce: Poem XLVI — The Cook Evening Stops
text:
The cook evening stops
+before the table where you ate;
+and starving to death your memory comes
+tasting not even water, out of sheer sadness.
+
+      But, as always, your humility consents
+to being offered the saddest kindness.
+And you will not taste, for you see who comes
+filially to the table where you ate.
+
+      The cook evening implores you
+and weeps for you in its still-sordid apron,
+which begins to love us from hearing us so much.
+
+      I make an effort too; for there is no
+courage to help oneself to these birds.
+Ah! We are going to help ourselves to nothing now.
editorial_note: The mother’s absent table is sustained through culinary verbs; tarde cocinera remains the stark cook evening, and birds hover between food, omens, and the courage no diner possesses.

title: Trilce: Poem XVII — This 2 Distills in a Single Batch
text:
This 2 distills in a single batch,
+and between us both we drain it.
+No one had heard me. Burning groove,
+civil abracadabra.
+
+The morning does not feel like the first,
+like the last stone ovulating
+by force of secrecy. The morning barefoot.
+The mud halfway
+between gray substances, more and less.
+Faces know nothing of the face, nor of the
+march toward encounters.
+And without a toward the exergue nods.
+The point of longing strays.
+
+June, you are ours. June, and on your shoulders
+I stand and roar with laughter, drying
+my meter and my pockets
+on your 21 seasonal nails.
+
+Good! Good!
editorial_note: The numeral remains an intimate substance consumed by two; ovulandas becomes ovulating without repairing its syntax, and sin hacia is kept as the absence of a directional toward.

title: Trilce: Poem XXXI — Hope Mourns among Cotton
text:
Hope mourns among cotton.
+
+Hoarse edges in uniform,
+of threats woven from magnificent spores
+with doormen, innate buttons.
+Do six suns rub against each other?
+Nativity. Be quiet, fear.
+
+A Christian, I hope, I always hope
+on my knees upon the circular stone that stands
+at the hundred corners of this fate
+so vague, where I peer out.
+
+And God, startled, grips
+our pulse, grave, mute,
+and like a father with his little girl,
+             barely,
+     only just, parts the bloody cotton
+and takes hope between his fingers.
+
+Lord, I want it…
+And enough!
editorial_note: Cotton moves between cloud, bandage, and childbirth; the uncertain se luden is rendered as mutual friction, while hope is both theological virtue and a small body delivered into God’s hand.

title: Gunwales of Ice
text:
I come to watch you pass every day,
+        enchanted little steamer, always far away…
+        Your eyes are two fair-haired captains;
+        your lip a very small red
+        handkerchief waving in a farewell of blood!
+
+
+        I come to watch you pass; until one day,
+        drunk on time and cruelty,
+        enchanted little steamer, always far away,
+        the evening star will set sail!
+        The rigging; treacherous winds; winds
+        of a woman who passed!
+        Your cold captains will give the order;
+        and the one who will have sailed away will be me…!
editorial_note: The distant woman and diminutive steamer remain superimposed; partir shifts from the evening star’s departure to the speaker’s final sailing.

title: Trilce: Poem XXXVII — I Met a Poor Young Woman
text:
I met a poor young woman
+whom I led as far as the stage.
+Her mother, her sisters, how kind, and also
+that unfortunate “you are not coming back” of hers.
+
+Since a certain business was going splendidly for me,
+they surrounded me with the air of a dynasty in bloom.
+The bride turned to water,
+and how well she used to weep for me
+her badly learned love.
+
+I liked her timid marinera,
+its humble ornaments as she made the turns,
+and how her handkerchief traced dots,
+accent marks, on the melography of her sedge-like dance.
+
+And when together we outwitted the parish priest,
+my business broke, and hers,
+and the swept-away sphere.
editorial_note: Marinera remains the named Peruvian dance, with its handkerchief writing musical punctuation; business, courtship, and cosmic sphere collapse together after the priest is deceived.

title: Trilce: Poem V — Dicotyledon Group
text:
Dicotyledon group. Petrels overture
+from it, propensities of trinity,
+endings that begin, ohs born of ayes
+one might think bevalued with heterogeneity.
+Group of the cotyledons!
+
+Let us see. Let that be, without being more.
+Let us see. Let it not transcend outward,
+and let it think as if not to be heard,
+and chrome itself and not be seen.
+And let it not gliss in the great collapse.
+
+The created voice rebels and refuses
+to be mesh, or love.
+Let bride and groom be bride and groom in eternity.
+For do not give 1, which will resound to infinity.
+And do not give 0, which will fall so silent
+until it wakes and sets 1 upright.
+
+Ah bicardiac group.
editorial_note: Vallejo’s verbs are recreated rather than regularized: petrels overture, forms bevalue, bodies chrome and gliss; the botanical pair becomes a two-hearted arithmetic of lovers.
